newsitem.title: ZAIRE: OAU welcomes rebel ceasefire in eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: OAU welcomes rebel ceasefire in eastern Zaire.

text.p: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) hailed a ceasefire announced by rebels in eastern Zaire on Monday and said it could open the way for negotiations on a political solution.
Muhamadu Bah, assistant secretary-general of the OAU, told Reuters the ceasefire declared by the rebels would ease tension in the Great Lakes region and help a regional summit in Kenya on Tuesday.
"It is a positive step indeed. The intention of our mission to Rwanda and Zaire was to secure a ceasefire," Bah told Reuters.

The ceasefire, due to start from 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) on Monday, was called by Laurent Kabila, leader of the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire. There was no immediate reaction from the government of Zaire.

Reuters correspondent Christian Jennings in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi bordering on the Zairean city of Goma said: "The ceasefire appears to be holding. There is absolutely no sound of gunfire."

Bah is a member of an OAU peace mission that opened talks in Rwanda on Monday aimed at securing a ceasefire in eastern Zaire between Zairean troops and the ethnic Tutsi rebels after two weeks of fighting. The mission is led by another OAU assistant secretary-general, Anatole Tiendrebeogo.
"A ceasefire is also good news because it will make it easy for negotiations to resume on a political settlement in Zaire. It also helps to reduce the tension in the region," Bah added.

Kabila, speaking by telephone from the rebel-held eastern Zairean city of Bukavu, said he had declared the ceasefire "because of the disquiet of the international community, to allow the International Red Cross to evacuate the refugees who want to return to their original countries".
"We hope that the unilateral ceasefire will be respected by the Zairean side. If they are against this decision, then combat will restart immediately," he added.

The Zairean renbel alliance is made up of Kabila's Popular Revolution Party (PRP), the National Council of Resistance for Democracy (NCRD), the Revolutionary Movement for the Liberation of Zaire (RMLZ) and the People's Democratic Alliance (PDA).

The parties have a long history of opposition to Zairean strongman Mobutu Sese Seko, who flew on Monday to the French Riviera capital of Nice from Switzerland, where he was undergoing treatment after surgery for cancer in August.

Fighting erupted when ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels took up arms against Zaire after local authorities in the eastern region issued an ultimatum to expel them back to Rwanda, which they left for Zaire as long ago as the end of the 18th century.
The OAU also wants the combatants in the Zaire conflict to pull back to their previous positions, a demand which political analysts said was likely to be rejected by the rebels.
Diplomats in Kigali doubted the effectiveness of the OAU mission, saying the pan-African body lacked the muscle to resolve the latest civil war on the world's poorest continent.
The OAU would also look into claims by Zaire that Rwandan troops were fighting alongside the rebels, Tiendrebeogo said.
Zaire has accused Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of aiding the rebels in the war but all three countries have denied the charges, saying the conflict was an internal Zairean matter.
A special envoy from the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees was expected in Kigali later on Monday to discuss plans to help the refugees trapped in the Zaire fighting.
Burundi's Defence Minister Firmin Sinzoyiheba, whose country is barred from the Nairobi summit because of regional sanctions, was also in Kigali for talks on the east Zaire crisis on Monday.
